canonicalExplanation.summary: A Java `String` is **immutable**: methods like `trim()`, `strip()`, `toUpperCase()` and `replace()` return **new** strings and never change the original, so you must use the result. Compare text with **`equals`** (or `equalsIgnoreCase`), never `==`, which compares **references** and can seem to work by accident with literals. When building text in a loop, `+=` creates a new string each time; use a **`StringBuilder`** instead. A `char` is a **UTF-16 code unit**, so some characters (many emoji) take **two** chars: `length()` counts code units, not user-visible characters.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
A learner's command parser does `if (input == "quit")`, which works when typed as a literal in tests but never matches real user input. They call `line.trim();` and wonder why spaces remain. Their report builds 50,000 lines with `+=` and takes seconds. A parser uses equals for tokens, strip for surrounding whitespace, and a StringBuilder to assemble an unknown number of output fragments. In this lesson you'll implement text parsing and construction while avoiding reference-equality and concatenation pitfalls.

examples.title: Parsing commands and building a report
examples.situation: A parser uses equals for tokens, strip for surrounding whitespace, and a StringBuilder to assemble an unknown number of output fragments.
walkthrough: **A parser uses equals for tokens:** equalsIgnoreCase("quit") matches typed input "  QUIT ".
**Strip for surrounding whitespace:** cmd = raw.strip() keeps the returned string.
**And a StringBuilder to assemble an unknown number of output fragments:** report(50_000) will append into one buffer instead of creating 50,000 strings.
examples.result: Commands match reliably and reports are built quickly.

examples.title: The trim that did nothing
examples.situation: A learner calls name.trim(); on its own line and saves names with spaces into a database.
walkthrough: String is immutable: trim returns a new string.
Write name = name.strip(); (strip also handles Unicode spaces).
examples.result: Saved names no longer have stray leading or trailing spaces.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: The == operator compares String text, and one char always represents one complete Unicode character.
misconceptions.correction: == compares object references, so use equals for text. A char is one UTF-16 code unit, and some characters need two.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In the opening story, why did input == "quit" never match?

analogy.example: A String is like **a printed card**: you can't erase it, only print a new one (strip returns a new card). == asks **"is this the same physical card?"**, while equals asks **"do they say the same thing?"**. A StringBuilder is **a whiteboard** you keep adding to before printing once.
limitations: Printing cards is cheap once, costly 50,000 times.
Some symbols need two squares on the card (surrogate pairs).

nearTransfer.prompt: Write countWords(String text) using strip and split("\\s+"), handling empty and all-space input. Then write joinWithCommas(String[] words) using StringBuilder without a trailing comma.

farTransfer.prompt: Write a tiny command interpreter that reads lines, supports "add N", "total" and "quit" (any case), rejects malformed lines with messages, and builds a transcript with StringBuilder. Test with odd spacing and capitalisation.

remediation.explanation: For every string operation ask: **am I comparing content (equals), keeping the returned value, and building in a loop (StringBuilder)?**
remediation.retryPrompt: Apply this to "The trim that did nothing".

recap.summary: To implement text parsing and construction, compare strings with equals or equalsIgnoreCase rather than ==, remember strings are immutable so assign the results of methods like strip, build text in loops with StringBuilder, and know that length counts UTF-16 code units rather than visible characters.
